options.text: a jury's refusal to consider novels written in languages that its members are unable to read
options.why: Paragraph 1 says four shortlisted books were written in languages the jury does not read, so the jury did consider them. The complaint is about credit, not exclusion.

options.text: a reviewer's claim that the prose of a translated novel belonged entirely to its original author
options.why: Reviewers who praise 'the author's luminous prose' appear in paragraph 5 as one general cause of invisibility. They are not the specific event in paragraph 1 that prompted the passage.

options.text: a prize announcement that credited authors and publishers while omitting the translators of most of the shortlisted books
options.why: Paragraph 1 describes the Ambervale Prize press release, which named six novels, authors and publishers but no translator. Four of the six books were translated, including one by the writer.

options.text: a publisher's decision to print the writer's name on an inside page rather than on the cover of a recent paperback
options.why: Paragraph 1 mentions the small typeface on page four only as a supporting illustration of the problem. The event that occasions the post is the shortlist press release, not one publisher's layout.

options.text: recasting the demand for credit as a chance for readers to acknowledge a debt they have unknowingly already incurred
options.why: The final sentence tells readers they 'have already loved a translator's work' and 'simply were not told whom to thank.' This turns the request into gratitude readers already owe rather than a new burden.

options.text: suggesting that readers who learn foreign languages will no longer need translators at all and can read the originals directly
options.why: The passage never proposes that readers learn languages or read originals. The appeal depends on readers continuing to rely on translations and simply naming the people who make them.

options.text: inviting readers to feel superior to the reviewers and prize juries who have so far failed to notice translators
options.why: Nothing in the final sentence sets readers against reviewers or juries. Those groups get their own instructions earlier in paragraph 6 ('If you run a prize,' 'If you review books'), and readers are addressed on their own terms.

options.text: warning readers that their admiration for foreign novels has been misdirected toward authors who did not deserve it
options.why: The sentence is warm and inclusive, not accusatory. Paragraph 6 opens by explicitly declining to diminish the author ('I am not asking for the author's name to be removed'), so the appeal does not suggest authors are undeserving.

options.text: consists mainly of publishers who must be persuaded that foreign books are easy to sell
options.why: Publishers' fears appear in paragraph 5 as a diagnosis, but paragraph 6 does not address publishers directly. Its 'If you' clauses name prizes, reviewers and readers.

options.text: shares the writer's expertise and already agrees that translators deserve to be named
options.why: The patient explanation of the plumbing misconception in paragraph 2 and the final reminder that readers 'were not told whom to thank' assume an audience that has not yet considered the issue.

options.text: is made up of fellow translators who need encouragement to abandon their habitual modesty
options.why: Translators' 'monkish modesty' is mentioned in paragraph 5 as one cause of the problem, but paragraph 6 addresses prize runners, reviewers and ordinary readers, not translators.

options.text: includes people in several different roles, each able to change one specific practice
options.why: The closing 'If you' sentences of paragraph 6 address, in turn, those who run prizes, those who review books, and readers, and they give each group a concrete action. This signals a mixed audience of readers and industry participants.

options.text: Because translators have cultivated a monkish modesty, they are themselves chiefly responsible for the convention that leaves their names off covers and press releases
options.why: Paragraph 5 does admit translators' modesty as a cause, but it is only one of three 'partly' causes. The thesis concerns authorship and credit, not blaming translators.

options.text: Because the English sentences of a translated novel are the translator's own decisions, the translator should be named as the person who wrote them
options.why: Paragraphs 2-3 establish that every English sentence is the translator's choice ('Every sentence the English reader admires, I wrote'). Paragraph 6 then concludes that a line on the cover should say 'who wrote the English sentences.'

options.text: Because publishers believe that foreign books are difficult to sell, translators will remain invisible until the economics of publishing and bookselling fundamentally change
options.why: Publishers' fear is only the first of three causes listed in paragraph 5, and the passage ends with a practical remedy, not resignation about economics.

options.text: Because translation changes every sentence of a novel, a translated book is essentially a new work that belongs to the translator rather than the author
options.why: Paragraphs 4 and 6 explicitly deny this. The writer did not invent the heroine, does not want credit for her, and is not asking for the author's name to be removed or shrunk.

options.text: acknowledge that publishers' concerns about cover design are legitimate and that translators should therefore accept credit on an inside page instead
options.why: Paragraph 6 asks for the translator's name 'on the front of the book,' so the writer rejects inside-page credit. Paragraph 1 already treated that kind of credit with irony.

options.text: forestall the fear that crediting translators would displace authors, so that the request that follows seems modest and easy to grant
options.why: The sentence rules out every version of the proposal that might threaten the author's standing. The next sentence then asks only for 'a line of type' the size of a blurb, which makes the demand hard to refuse.

options.text: introduce a new counterargument about shared authorship that the remaining sentences of the paragraph then refute point by point in detail
options.why: The rest of paragraph 6 states the proposal and assigns actions. It does not refute a counterargument point by point, and the objection about shared credit is dismissed within the quoted sentence itself.

options.text: concede that the original author contributes more to a novel than the translator does and therefore deserves a larger share of the credit
options.why: The sentence limits what is being requested and does not weigh the relative size of contributions. Paragraph 3 has already claimed full authorship of the English sentences.

options.text: Paragraph 2 shows a single forced choice in one sentence, and paragraph 3 multiplies that choice across the whole novel to claim its sentences
options.why: Paragraph 2 isolates one decision about 'the weather.' Paragraph 3 opens with 'Consider the scale of the problem' and multiplies roughly forty decisions a page by three hundred pages, concluding 'Every sentence the English reader admires, I wrote.'

options.text: Paragraph 2 describes the writer's personal method, and paragraph 3 shifts to statistics gathered from a survey of other translators to generalize it
options.why: The count in paragraph 3 is the writer's own 'rough count' of her own work on Aalvik's novel. No survey, other translators or outside data appear.

options.text: Paragraph 2 argues that translation is impossible, and paragraph 3 reverses course to show that most of the novel's sentences survive translation intact
options.why: Paragraph 3 says the English book 'shares none of its sentences' with the Norwegian one. It intensifies, rather than reverses, the point that sentences are remade.

options.text: Paragraph 2 presents the popular view of translation, and paragraph 3 offers a competing popular view, held by reviewers, that the writer also rejects
options.why: Paragraph 3 does not present another popular view, from reviewers or anyone else. It builds on the writer's own account in paragraph 2 by counting the decisions across a whole novel.

options.text: treating the translator's authorship as settled by the preceding paragraphs and turning the argument toward the causes of a problem
options.why: The word 'then' assumes paragraphs 2-4 have established authorship. The question moves the passage from proving the claim to diagnosing why credit is withheld, and the rest of paragraph 5 answers it.

options.text: signaling that the writer will now abandon personal experience in favor of a survey of publishing history and its contracts
options.why: Paragraph 5 still speaks personally ('I confess') and offers three present-day causes. It gives no history of publishing or its contracts.

options.text: introducing the specific remedy that paragraph 6 will later request from prize committees, reviewers, and ordinary readers of translated fiction
options.why: The question asks for causes, which paragraph 5 supplies. The remedy appears only in paragraph 6, after the diagnosis is complete.

options.text: reopening the objection from paragraph 4 so that the writer can concede that the convention has some justification
options.why: Paragraph 4 ends with the rebuttal 'Architecture is credited; so is the building.' The question does not revive the objection; it asks why a practice already shown to be unjust continues.

options.text: interrupt the argument with a digression about building so that the reader forgets the objection raised earlier in the paragraph
options.why: The carpenter sentence extends the objection's own image from earlier in paragraph 4 ('a skilled carpenter working from her drawings') in order to answer it. The structure engages the objection rather than evading it.

options.text: accumulate the carpenter's contributions in subordinate clauses before the brief main clause, so the modest conclusion seems earned
options.why: The sentence delays its main verb while two relative clauses pile up the carpenter's choices and the client's long residence. The short ending 'is not usually left off the plaque' then lands as an understated, well-supported verdict.

options.text: place the main claim first and then qualify it with a list of exceptions in which carpenters do go uncredited
options.why: The main claim comes last, not first. The listed items are the carpenter's contributions, which support credit; they are not exceptions that withhold it.

options.text: balance two equal independent clauses so that the carpenter's labor and the architect's design receive matching emphasis
options.why: The sentence has a single main clause with subordinate modifiers. The balanced two-clause structure appears instead in the paragraph's final sentence, 'Architecture is credited; so is the building.'

options.text: Weil's reporting is the book's 'great strength' because its figures are so grim
options.why: The training figure comes from the writer's own experience, not from Weil's reporting, and it serves her critique rather than her praise.

options.text: 'The people were there all along' but had been 'priced out of serving'
options.why: That claim appears in paragraph 5 and is supported by the Tillery County roster figures, not by the training requirement.

options.text: The volunteer model is 'simply obsolete' because workers no longer live or work near their local station
options.why: This is Weil's diagnosis, which the writer is rebutting; the training hours support her counter-explanation, not his.

options.text: The volunteer system has been 'quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry'
options.why: The training detail comes right after the claim that the system has been 'quietly loaded with burdens it was never designed to carry.' It is the first of two burdens (training, then self-funded equipment) that illustrate that claim.

options.text: accept the factual basis of Weil's argument in order to isolate and dispute the conclusion he draws from it
options.why: The concession admits the changed work pattern Weil describes, and the next sentence pivots with 'But obsolete is the wrong word,' narrowing the disagreement to the diagnosis.

options.text: illustrate with a vivid example how far volunteers now commute, reinforcing Weil's point that distance alone explains the decline
options.why: The example is vivid, but its purpose is to set up the rebuttal that follows, not to strengthen Weil's case. The writer goes on to blame burdens, not distance alone.

options.text: signal that the writer's own experience is dated and that Weil's more recent reporting should be trusted
options.why: The writer goes on to cite her own experience of training hours and fundraising as authoritative; nothing suggests she defers to Weil.

options.text: concede that the volunteer model cannot survive and shift the argument toward how paid crews should be funded
options.why: The writer explicitly denies that the model is obsolete and never endorses paid crews; the concession is limited to the work pattern.

options.text: It demonstrates that fire companies, like pools, should charge the public user fees for the protection they provide rather than rely on county taxes
options.why: The analogy ridicules making the lifeguard raise pool money. It argues against self-funding, not for fees, and the writer actually favors a county levy.

options.text: It provides a second case study that, like Tillery County, shows what happens to a volunteer roster when public money covers equipment costs
options.why: The lifeguard is a hypothetical comparison, not evidence; the only case study is Tillery County in paragraph 5.

options.text: It lightens the tone with much-needed humor after the grim statistics of paragraph 2, reassuring readers that the crisis is far less serious than Weil's reporting suggests
options.why: The writer never minimizes the crisis; she calls Weil's warning 'overdue' and uses the analogy to sharpen criticism, not to reassure.

options.text: It transfers a familiar arrangement into a setting where its unfairness is immediately visible, preparing the reader to see fundraising as a structural failure
options.why: Paragraph 4 says 'The absurdity would be obvious anywhere else' and then calls fundraising 'the structural failure it is'; the analogy makes a burden people have gotten used to look absurd.

options.text: summarize the argument of paragraphs 1 and 2 before the writer turns to introducing the Tillery County evidence
options.why: The sentence looks forward to the critique in paragraph 3, not to the evidence in paragraph 5, and it summarizes nothing.

options.text: soften the criticism that follows by acknowledging that every book, however well reported, has a few minor weaknesses
options.why: The sentence is blunt rather than softening, and the flaw it names, the diagnosis, is the book's central argument, not a minor weakness.

options.text: announce that the writer will dispute the accuracy of the numbers reported in paragraph 2, beginning with the roster figures
options.why: The writer never challenges the figures, including the roster numbers; she treats them as 'the shape of the thing' and attacks only the conclusion drawn from them.

options.text: mark the turn from praise to critique while confining the disagreement to Weil's interpretation rather than his facts
options.why: It follows paragraph 2's praise of the reporting and introduces the critique; the word 'diagnosis' limits the objection to Weil's reading of the evidence, which the rest of the paragraph pursues.

options.text: balancing two independent clauses of equal weight to present apathy and overwork as two competing explanations
options.why: Apathy is rejected in the previous sentence; this sentence offers a single explanation, not two balanced alternatives.

options.text: stacking the roles in a series before the final clause, so that the bewilderment it describes seems unwarranted
options.why: The four-item list piles up the demands, and the delayed 'and then wondered' lands after the pile, exposing the gap between what was asked and the surprise at the result.

options.text: repeating the word 'we' to shift blame onto the volunteers themselves for taking on too much
options.why: 'We' refers to the community and system that made demands, and the blame falls on the burdens imposed, not on the volunteers.

options.text: placing the cause first and the effect last to suggest the loss of volunteers was entirely unforeseeable
options.why: The sentence implies the opposite: given the demands listed, the outcome should have been obvious.

options.text: set two matched clauses side by side so the gap between the turnouts conveys how unpredictable a response can be
options.why: The semicolon joins parallel clauses without a connecting word, letting the contrast between nine and three stand starkly and illustrating the 'arithmetic' the writer says Weil understands.

options.text: create a pause that signals the writer's shift from personal memory of the pager to discussion of Weil's book
options.why: The shift to the book occurs in the next sentence, not at the semicolon, which sits inside a description of turnout.

options.text: introduce an explanation of why fewer volunteers appear on certain nights, such as late shifts or distant jobs
options.why: No explanation follows the semicolon, only a second instance; causes such as distant jobs are not discussed until paragraph 3.

options.text: subordinate the second clause to the first, implying that three responders is the more typical turnout on most nights
options.why: A semicolon links independent clauses of equal weight; neither clause is subordinated, and the sentence gives no sense of which turnout is typical.

options.text: distrust of small towns that neglect essential services until an emergency forces them to act
options.why: The fire department is presented as a successful model, not as an example of neglect.

options.text: belief that people exposed to a shared danger owe one another participation rather than payment
options.why: The analogy stresses that the people whose houses would burn show up for drills instead of mailing a check, modeling the claim that obligation should attach to dependence and be paid in hours.

options.text: assumption that institutions employing ninety engineers can easily afford the modest sponsorship stipends Alcock proposes
options.why: The bank example concerns a failure to assign hours, and the fire department analogy argues against checks, not for affordable ones.

options.text: admiration for individuals who keep doing dangerous unpaid work out of stubbornness after their neighbors stop helping
options.why: The analogy rejects reliance on the one person who owns a hose; stubborn individuals are what the writer wants to stop depending on.

options.text: return to the load-bearing metaphor in order to restate the diagnosis of hidden dependence offered in paragraph 2
options.why: The sentence does reuse the wall image, but its purpose is to bound and defend the cure, not to restate the diagnosis.

options.text: signal that the writer has come to doubt whether institutions will contribute hours at all, even under pressure
options.why: The sentence ends with a confident claim that the proposal would spread the weight; it qualifies scope, not conviction.

options.text: concede that Alcock's sponsorship model remains necessary as a fallback for the smallest and most neglected libraries
options.why: The sentence says small libraries will rely on individual stubbornness; it does not reintroduce sponsorship as a fallback.

options.text: limit the reach of the proposal so that it cannot be dismissed for failing to solve every case
options.why: The writer concedes that the smallest libraries will still depend on individuals, then reasserts the proposal's main benefit of spreading the weight; the qualification preempts an objection.

options.text: retracting her earlier judgment that the second half of the book loses its footing when it turns to remedies
options.why: The sentence introduces the alternative to Alcock's cure; it sustains, rather than withdraws, the criticism of the second half.

options.text: conceding that her proposal is less original than Alcock's and therefore less likely to be adopted
options.why: Locating the cure in his margins does not weaken her proposal; the writer calls it the better cure and argues for it confidently.

options.text: presenting her alternative as consistent with Alcock's own evidence rather than as a rejection of his project
options.why: By locating the cure inside the book, the writer frames her disagreement as completing Alcock's work with his own material, which keeps her praise of the first half credible.

options.text: suggesting that Alcock deliberately suppressed a conclusion that would have displeased the corporate sponsors he praises
options.why: Nothing in the passage attributes motive or suppression to Alcock; the writer calls his faith in a check puzzling, not dishonest.

options.text: proving that maintainers would refuse payment if it were offered to them, preferring to keep their work a gift
options.why: The analogy says nothing about refusal; the writer even grants that stipends have saved projects.

options.text: contrasting neighborly generosity with the hostility of the bug reports described in paragraph 4 to shame ungrateful users
options.why: The analogy is about what payment does to a gift, and it precedes the bug report testimony rather than contrasting with it.

options.text: supplying a documented case in which sponsorship caused a volunteer to abandon a project she had long maintained
options.why: The neighbor is a hypothetical illustration, not a documented case, and the neighbor does not quit; the point is the changed relationship.

options.text: rendering an abstract claim about payment and obligation in a scene readers can test against their own experience
options.why: The analogy makes concrete the claim that a stipend changes what the work is, showing how paying converts a gift into a service and gives the payer the right to complain.

options.text: how a service, a problem, and a right are three separate benefits the neighbor gains from being paid
options.why: Only the last clause names a right, and it belongs to the payer, not the neighbor; the series records losses of the gift character, not benefits.

options.text: how uncertain it is whether the neighbor will continue shoveling the shared walkway once money becomes involved in the arrangement
options.why: The parallel declaratives are flatly certain; nothing in the structure conveys doubt about continuation.

options.text: how a single act of payment sets off a chain of consequences that ends with the payer entitled to complain
options.why: The introductory time clause marks the one triggering moment, and the three parallel main clauses accumulate consequences, with the final one landing on the payer's new entitlement.

options.text: how the neighbor's labor grows heavier with each winter that she is left to shovel the walkway entirely alone
options.why: The clauses describe changes in the relationship after payment, not increasing physical labor over years.

options.text: softens the review's criticism by implying that the writer herself once favored the corporate sponsorship Alcock recommends
options.why: Nothing suggests the writer ever favored sponsorship; the shared failing is not noticing dependence, not endorsing a check.

options.text: places the writer alongside her readers among those responsible, so the proposal reads as shared duty rather than accusation
options.why: By counting herself among the dependents who failed to notice, the writer turns the final charge into a collective admission, which suits an argument that obligation attaches to dependence.

options.text: directs the closing sentences specifically at Alcock as the one reader most in need of correction
options.why: The plural widens the address to everyone who ran code on the walls; Alcock is not singled out in these sentences.

options.text: separates the writer and her fellow maintainers from the banks and hospitals that profit from their unpaid labor without noticing
options.why: The pronoun includes the writer with the dependents who were standing on the work, not with the maintainers set apart from the institutions that profit.

options.text: A local institution has circulated a pledge whose practice the writer supports but whose wording she believes misplaces responsibility.
options.why: Paragraph 1 names the exact unease: she "agrees with a proposal and distrusts its wording," and then asks who "had taken it from them."

options.text: A library newsletter has reported that the town's children spend more hours on screens than their parents did at that age.
options.why: Paragraph 1 mentions the newsletter only as the other thing in the envelope. The passage never reports or compares children's screen hours.

options.text: A reader of the magazine has argued publicly that the writer's own family history offers no guidance for households today.
options.why: No reader challenges the writer anywhere. The occasion is the pledge card arriving in the library's envelope (paragraph 1).

options.text: A local institution has asked households to give up their devices entirely, a demand the writer considers unrealistic for modern families.
options.why: The card asks only for "Screens Down at Supper" (paragraph 1). Nothing suggests a demand to give up devices, and paragraph 3 notes that each machine "stayed."

options.text: They are tolerable for adults, who can regulate themselves, but harmful to children until they learn restraint.
options.why: The passage keeps placing the problem with adults: the grandfather in paragraph 2, "Dad included" in paragraph 3, and the adult reader told to put the phone away in paragraph 6. It does not blame children who must learn restraint.

options.text: They are each less disruptive than the one before, so households now have little reason to regulate them.
options.why: The writer presents the pattern as repeating and still needed ("The pattern repeated itself"; "The machine has changed. The fence has not."). She never ranks the machines by how disruptive they are.

options.text: They are welcome once the household, adults included, decides when they may and may not have its attention.
options.why: Paragraph 3 describes telling "the stranger when to call" and marking off a single hour. Paragraph 6 tells the adult reader to sit down with the "phone in the drawer."

options.text: They are intrusions that a careful household should keep out of the home as long as it reasonably can.
options.why: Paragraph 3 says the household "did not bar the stranger" and that each machine "stayed." The writer never recommends keeping machines out.

options.text: the family's supper rule, across generations, bound the adults of the household as explicitly as it bound the young
options.why: "Dad included" echoes paragraph 2, where the grandmother built the fence "to keep herself and her husband inside." This shows the rule still applied to adults in 1967.

options.text: the grandmother's rule had failed by the next generation and had to be written down again from scratch
options.why: Paragraph 3 presents the new entry as "The pattern repeated itself," which is continuity, not failure. The writer calls the repetition instructive, not a collapse.

options.text: television proved more tempting to the family than the radio or telephone had been, requiring the strongest wording yet
options.why: The passage never compares how strongly each machine pulled at the family. The entry names the father, which parallels the radio story in paragraph 2. It does not rank the devices.

options.text: the household's rules grew stricter with each new machine as the children became teenagers and harder to keep at the table
options.why: Nothing indicates the rules got stricter over time. Paragraph 3 stresses that the household did "the same thing" each time.

options.text: Paragraph 2 relies on family memory, and paragraph 3 corrects that memory with written records from the ledgers.
options.why: Both paragraphs draw on ledgers and memory alike: the grandmother's ledger and "The family story" in paragraph 2, and the mother's memory and ledger in paragraph 3. Paragraph 3 does not correct paragraph 2.

options.text: Paragraph 2 narrates the grandmother's rule, and paragraph 3 defines the terms that make the rule a ritual rather than a curfew.
options.why: The definitions of curfew and ritual come in paragraph 4. Paragraph 3 continues the narrative pattern rather than defining terms.

options.text: Paragraph 2 presents a single founding example, and paragraph 3 shows that the household's response recurred with each later machine.
options.why: Paragraph 3 opens with "The pattern repeated itself" and then lists the telephone and the television, each met with the same scheduling response the grandmother set up in paragraph 2.

options.text: Paragraph 2 describes a rule that worked, and paragraph 3 explains why later generations found it impossible to maintain.
options.why: Paragraph 3 shows the rule being renewed, not abandoned. The 1967 entry, "Set off at supper, no exceptions," repeats the grandmother's rule.

options.text: shifts the argument from the family's history to the reader's household before the final paragraph begins
options.why: The turn to the reader comes in paragraph 6 with "I would urge you." This sentence stays within the evaluation of the family's recorded suppers.

options.text: introduces new ledger evidence that contradicts the letters describing sullen, silent meals and proves the suppers were cheerful
options.why: No new ledger evidence appears. The next sentence offers the mother's memory of "The sullen suppers of 1941," which confirms rather than contradicts that the meals were sullen.

options.text: accepts the narrowed claim of the previous sentence and then asserts that the narrowed claim still carries weight
options.why: The previous sentence reduces the hour's benefit to "attendance." This sentence accepts that reduction with "But" and "not nothing," and the next sentence gives the memory evidence that attendance is what lasted.

options.text: withdraws the preceding concession and reasserts that the quiet hour did in fact produce lively family conversation after all
options.why: The writer never takes back the admission. Paragraph 5 grants that the hour "produced attendance" only, and it goes on calling the suppers "sullen."

options.text: balancing two independent clauses of equal weight, so that the parent's action and the child's observation appear as separate obligations owed by different members of the household
options.why: The clauses are linked commands aimed at the same adult reader. The child's role is only to see the adult; nothing gives the child an obligation.

options.text: placing a series of imperatives first and the "until" clause last, so that the actions lead toward an end point in which the rule's original target is forgotten
options.why: The commands come first, interrupted by "phone in the drawer" and "every night." The final subordinate clause names the outcome, shared ownership and no memory of whom the rule protected, which answers the question in paragraph 1.

options.text: repeating the word "you" at the start of each clause, so that the reader is singled out as the person the pledge was designed to protect
options.why: "You" does not open the clauses, and the sentence ends by saying nobody remembers whom the rule protected. The reader is addressed as the adult who must comply, not as the protected party.

options.text: opening with a dependent clause that states the goal, so that the commands which follow appear as mere suggestions the reader may accept or ignore at will
options.why: The sentence begins with commands ("Sit down," "let them see you"), not with a dependent clause. The "until" clause comes last.

options.text: Shielded fixtures would cut crime on Cutler Avenue by half, making it the safest street in all of Larkhaven within a year.
options.why: Makes a sweeping claim about crime with no evidence anywhere in the testimony.

options.text: Because shielded fixtures send that wasted light down to the pavement, Cutler Avenue would stay just as bright where walkers and drivers need it.
options.why: It answers the safety worry directly and ties it to sentence 9's point about misdirected light.

options.text: Many members of our club also enjoy photographing the moon and planets, which look far clearer in a dark sky than under the white globes on Cutler.
options.why: Moves to a hobby detail and never takes up the safety concern.

options.text: Honestly, anyone who thinks a dark sky makes streets dangerous has probably never stood in our library lot after sunset on a clear night.
options.why: Dismisses the council's concern instead of answering it, which would alienate the audience she needs to persuade.

options.text: Skies across the whole region have grown brighter for decades as towns and highways have expanded in every direction.
options.why: Points to regional growth as a cause, which weakens the claim that the Cutler globes are responsible.

options.text: Our club has grown from six members to more than forty, and most new members are families from the east side of town.
options.why: Club details stay on the topic but give no evidence about what is causing the problem.

options.text: Last October, when an outage darkened Cutler Avenue for one night, our members found Andromeda from the same lot within minutes.
options.why: With only the globes removed, the galaxy came back, which isolates the lights as the cause.

options.text: Andromeda is about two and a half million light-years away, which makes it one of the most distant objects visible to the eye.
options.why: A general astronomy fact about the galaxy; it says nothing about what caused the loss.

options.text: The problem is not that the lights are on but that they point the wrong way.
options.why: Both halves are "that" clauses, so the construction is parallel and the meaning is clear.

options.text: The problem is not that the lights are on, but, where exactly they point.
options.why: Adds commas that don't belong and still leaves the halves unparallel.

options.text: The problem is not the lights being on but that they are pointed wrongly.
options.why: Changes the wording, but it now pairs a noun phrase with a clause and is still not parallel.

options.text: The problem is not that the lights are on but their pointing the wrong way.
options.why: Pairs a "that" clause with a gerund phrase, so the halves are still not parallel.

options.text: Erosion is a serious problem in Merrow Point, and over the past three decades the town has tried several different ways to deal with its slowly retreating coastline.
options.why: Almost no one would dispute it, and it does not preview a line of reasoning.

options.text: Dune restoration and relocation have both failed to slow the losses, so the town should extend the Pell Street seawall north along Gannet Road to protect every home.
options.why: It contradicts the report's evidence and its recommendation.

options.text: Because the seawall has cost the town its beach while dunes and relocation have slowed the losses, Merrow Point should fund those approaches instead of more concrete.
options.why: It makes an arguable claim and follows the report's order: seawall, dunes and relocation, recommendation.

options.text: This report describes the concrete seawall, the planted dunes at Little Cove, the relocated pump station and the movable lifeguard tower along Gannet Road in Merrow Point.
options.why: It lists the topics but makes no arguable claim.

options.text: The seawall at Pell Street was built in 1998, back when many residents and council members believed that concrete walls were the best option for the shoreline.
options.why: It goes back over the seawall's history and does not interpret the dune data.

options.text: This proves that dunes will completely stop erosion everywhere along the Merrow Point shoreline for good, so the town will never need to move another building.
options.why: One season of data at one site cannot show that erosion will stop everywhere or that relocation will never be needed.

options.text: Losing a few inches instead of two feet suggests the planted dunes are taking in wave energy that the bare bluff near the wall cannot.
options.why: It interprets the comparison and links it to the claim that dunes work better.

options.text: We took these measurements with survey stakes on three separate mornings in late October and early November, recording each reading in a shared class notebook.
options.why: It describes the method instead of explaining what the data mean for the claim.

options.text: The board should fund us because next year we will surely win the whole Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore and bring home its trophy.
options.why: Makes a promise the report gives no evidence for, and it ignores the board's values.

options.text: The board should fund us because the team had so much fun this year and would love to keep the good times going.
options.why: Hints at enthusiasm, but it says nothing about learning or careful spending.

options.text: The board should fund us because robotics is clearly more exciting than the other clubs asking for money this spring.
options.why: Keeps the competitive, boastful appeal instead of pointing to the board's values.

options.text: The board should fund us because steady attendance and new skills came from very little money, and the funding would build on both.
options.why: Names all three of the board's values (participation, learning, frugality) and links them to the request.

options.text: I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked new clubs for a summary, and these results bear directly on its budget vote.
options.why: Keeps the exigence and states outright that the report's results bear on the board's vote.

options.text: I am writing it because the board asked, though honestly most of what we did is easier to show than to explain.
options.why: Undercuts the report and is too casual for this audience.

options.text: I am writing it because the Student Activities Board, which meets monthly in the library, likes to keep paper records of every club.
options.why: Adds a trivial detail about the board instead of linking the report to the vote.

options.text: I am writing it because my adviser said that writing reports is good practice for college applications and scholarship essays later on.
options.why: Swaps in a personal reason that has nothing to do with the board's decision.

options.text: Ms. Delacroix-Tam also teaches two sections of chemistry, coaches the debate team, and helps supervise the science fair each spring.
options.why: Moves the focus to the adviser's other duties and draws no link to the funding argument.

options.text: Because attendance stayed above nine, the club will certainly grow to more than twenty members by next fall, doubling its size.
options.why: Predicts with certainty something the evidence does not support.

options.text: Exam week this year fell in the middle of January, which is earlier than usual for Harlow Creek High School.
options.why: Adds a side detail about the calendar instead of explaining the evidence.

options.text: That consistency suggests the money would serve a committed group rather than a club that fades once the novelty wears off.
options.why: Explains what the attendance shows (commitment) and links it to the funding argument by answering the worry that a new club may not last.

options.text: If you have ever cut through the Brambleton cul-de-sacs on your way to school, you have walked past a field of cattails and cracked pipe that few of us have noticed.
options.why: Speaks directly to student readers through a familiar route and still sets up the field that sentence 2 identifies as the marsh.

options.text: Finch Lane residents still remember the two days of rain last April, when water crept up to their doorsteps and their basements had to be pumped out.
options.why: Moves the flooding evidence in sentence 6 to the start, so the field that sentence 2 calls Cutler's Marsh is never introduced.

options.text: Honestly, most of us could not care less about some swampy old field behind a subdivision somewhere, but maybe we should start caring about it a little.
options.why: Too casual and dismissive for a paper read by parents and teachers, and it never names the place.

options.text: Since the beginning of human history, people everywhere have drained wetlands for farms, roads and towns, and they have often come to regret the choices they made.
options.why: A sweeping historical claim that loses the local, familiar hook and the specific field.

options.text: At that rate, the 180,000-dollar restoration would cost about as much as three floods like last April's, and the town would not have to pay it again.
options.why: Uses the figures from sentences 4 and 6 to answer a cost worry with a comparison taxpayers can follow.

options.text: Restoring the marsh would also save the town money on mowing, road salt and school supplies for many decades after the project is finally done.
options.why: Claims savings that nothing in the draft backs up, and school supplies have nothing to do with the project.

options.text: The water on Finch Lane was muddy and cold, and several families had to haul couches, beds and boxes to the upper floors of their homes that weekend.
options.why: Adds vivid detail about the flood but says nothing about cost to taxpayers.

options.text: Parents should simply stop worrying about money, because protecting nature is always worth whatever it ends up costing the town and the taxpayers who live there.
options.why: Brushes off the audience's concern instead of answering it, and the claim is not supported.

options.text: The town should pay to restore Cutler's Marsh, mainly because doing so would finally put an end to the flooding on Finch Lane.
options.why: Takes a position but previews only flooding, leaving out mosquitoes and the lab.

options.text: The town should pay to restore Cutler's Marsh, because it would ease flooding, keep mosquitoes in check and give our biology classes an outdoor lab.
options.why: Takes an arguable position and previews flooding, mosquitoes and the lab, in the order the paragraphs follow.

options.text: Although restoring Cutler's Marsh would ease flooding, the high costs and the swarms of mosquitoes mean the town council should think twice before approving it.
options.why: Argues against the plan the editorial supports.

options.text: Cutler's Marsh was once home to many plants and animals, and people in Larkfield have had different opinions about its future over time.
options.why: States no position and previews none of the editorial's points.

options.text: The ditches dug forty years ago, though, are the reason the field is so dry and cracked today, as readers may recall.
options.why: Looks back to sentence 2's history and never ties the sponge to the April flooding.

options.text: Many other towns across the state have restored marshes over the years, and residents there are often quite proud of the work they did.
options.why: Changes the subject to other towns instead of explaining the connection.

options.text: Had the marsh been holding water last April, much of that rain would have soaked into it slowly instead of rushing toward Finch Lane.
options.why: Applies the sponge comparison to the April flood, linking the evidence to the claim.

options.text: Sponges are simple sea animals, and some kinds can soak up many times their own weight in seawater before they slowly squeeze it back out.
options.why: Picks up the word sponge but drifts to biology facts with no link to the flood.

options.text: A developer forty years ago drained a field for houses that were never built that lies behind the Brambleton subdivision and was once Cutler's Marsh.
options.why: Keeps the facts, but the modifiers are misplaced, so it sounds as if the houses lie behind the subdivision.

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision there lies, past the very last cul-de-sac, a field that in the past, about forty years ago, was once Cutler's Marsh.
options.why: Wordy and repetitive, and it leaves out the developer's draining.

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision lies a field of cattails that was, forty years ago, Cutler's Marsh, until a developer drained it for houses never built.
options.why: Keeps the location, the history and the cause in one clear, concise sentence.

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision lies a field, it was Cutler's Marsh forty years ago, until a developer drained it for houses that were never built.
options.why: A comma splice joins two independent clauses.
